pages.caption: And many a hunting song they sung, And song of game and glee.
Then tuned to plaintive strains their tongue, "Of Scotland's luve and lee."
pages.scene: Song title displayed in ornate lettering

pages.caption: To wilder measures next they turn "The Black, Black Bull of Norroway!"
pages.scene: Dark musical performance with dramatic tones

pages.caption: Sudden the tapers cease to burn, The minstrels cease to play.
pages.scene: Candles flickering and minstrels falling silent

pages.caption: "The Cout of Keeldar," by J. Leyden.
In Norroway, langsyne, there lived a certain lady, and she had three dochters.
The auldest o' them said to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast
pages.scene: Young woman speaking to her mother

pages.caption: me a collop, for I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
pages.scene: Young woman speaking to her mother

pages.caption: Her mither did sae.
And the dochter gaed awa' to an auld witch washerwife and telled her purpose.
The auld wife bade her stay that day, and gang and look out o' her
pages.scene: Old woman gazing through back door

pages.caption: back door,
pages.scene: Old woman gazing through back door

pages.caption: and see what she could see.
pages.scene: Old woman gazing through back door

pages.caption: She saw nocht the first day.
pages.scene: First daughter looking but seeing nothing

pages.caption: The second day she did the same, and saw nocht.
On the third day she looked again, and saw a coach-and-six coming along the road.
She ran in and telled the auld wife what she saw.
"Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you."
Sae they took her into the coach, and galloped aff.
The second dochter next says to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast
me a collop, fur I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
Her mither did sae; and awa' she gaed to the auld wife, as her sister
had dune.
On the third day she looked out o' the back door, and saw a coach-and-four
coming along the road.
"Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you." Sae they took her in, and aff
they set.
The third dochter says to her mither: "Mither, bake me a bannock, and roast me
a collop,
for I'm gaun awa' to seek my fortune."
Her mither did sae; and awa' she gaed to the auld witch-wife.
She bade her look out o' her back door, and see what she could see.
pages.description: [old wife points to the back door]

pages.caption: She did sae; and when she came back said she saw nocht.
pages.scene: Third daughter looking but seeing nothing

pages.caption: The second day she did the same, and saw nocht.
pages.scene: Still no sighting the second day

pages.caption: The third day she looked again, and on coming back said to the auld wife
pages.description: [daughter speaks with fear in her voice]
pages.scene: Black bull appearing on the road

pages.caption: she saw nocht but a muckle Black Bull coming roaring alang the road.
pages.description: [massive black bull charges down the road]
pages.scene: Black bull appearing on the road

pages.caption: "Aweel," quo' the auld wife, "yon's for you."
pages.scene: Old wife declares the bull for her

pages.caption: On hearing this she was next to distracted wi' grief and terror; but she was
lifted up and set on his back, and awa' they went.
pages.description: [bull carries her away into the wild]

pages.caption: Aye they traveled, and on they traveled, till the lady grew faint wi' hunger.
pages.scene: Bull traveling with lady on back

pages.caption: "Eat out o' my right lug," says the Black Bull, "and drink out o' my
left lug,
and set by your leavings."
pages.description: [food and drink appear from the ear]

pages.caption: Sae she did as he said, and was wonderfully refreshed.
And lang they gaed, and sair they rade, till they came in sight o' a
very big and bonny castle.
"Yonder we maun be this night," quo' the bull; "for my auld brither lives yonder."
And presently they were at the place.
They lifted her aff his back, and took her in, and sent him away to
pages.description: [servants lift her down from the bull]

pages.caption: a park for the night.
In the morning, when they brought the bull hame, they took the lady into a
fine shining parlor.
And gave her a beautiful apple, telling her no to break it till she was
in the greatest strait ever mortal was in in the world, and that wad bring
her o't.
Again she was lifted on the bull's back.
pages.description: [lady mounted once more on the bull]

pages.caption: And after she had ridden far, and farer than I can tell, they came in
pages.description: [bull and lady ride through wild landscape]

pages.caption: sight o' a far bonnier castle, and far farther awa' than the last.
Says the bull till her: "Yonder we maun be the night, for my second brither
lives yonder."
And they were at the place directly.
They lifted her down and took her in, and sent the bull to the field
pages.scene: Sent to field for the night

pages.caption: for the night.
pages.scene: Sent to field for the night

pages.caption: In the morning they took the lady into a fine and rich room.
And gave her the finest pear she had ever seen, bidding her no to break
it till she was in the greatest strait ever mortal could be in, and that
wad get her out o't.
Again she was lifted and set on his back, and awa' they went.
pages.scene: Set upon bull for third journey

pages.caption: And lang they gaed, and sair they rade, till they came in sight o' the
far biggest castle, and far farthest aff, they had yet seen.
"We maun be yonder the night," says the bull, "for my young brither lives yonder."
And they were there directly.
They lifted her down, took her in, and sent the bull to the field for
the night.
pages.description: [bull stands in the field at nightfall]

pages.caption: In the morning they took her into a room, the finest of a'.
And gied her a plum, telling her no to break it till she was in
the greatest strait mortal could be in, and that wad get her out o't.
Presently they brought hame the bull, set the lady on his back, and awa' they
went.
And aye they gaed, and on they rade, till they came to a dark and
ugsome glen,
where they stopped, and the lady lighted down.
Says the bull to her: "Here ye maun stay till I gang and fight the
deil."
Ye maun seat yoursel' on that stane, and move neither hand nor fit till I
come back,
else I'll never find ye again.
And if everything round about ye turns blue I hae beated the deil; but should
a' things turn red he'll hae conquered me.
pages.description: [clash of horns echoes through the glen]

pages.caption: She set hersel' down on the stane, and by-and-by a' round her turned blue.
pages.scene: Lady sits on stone, world turns blue

pages.caption: O'ercome wi' joy, she lifted the ae fit and crossed it owre the ither, sae
glad was she that her companion was victorious.
The bull returned and sought for but never could find her.
pages.scene: Bull returns but cannot find her

pages.caption: Lang she sat, and aye she grat, till she wearied.
At last she rase and gaed awa', she kedna whaur till.
On she wandered till she came to a great hill o' glass, that she tried
a' she could to climb, bat wasna able.
Round the bottom o' the hill she gaed, sabbing and seeking a passage owre, till
pages.description: [lady circles the base of the hill]

pages.caption: at last she came to a smith's house.
And the smith promised, if she wad serve him seven years, he wad make her
iron shoon,
wherewi' she could climb owre the glassy hill.
At seven years' end she got her iron shoon.
pages.description: [lady receives iron shoes from the smith]

pages.caption: Clamb the glassy hill, and chanced to come to the auld washerwife's habitation.
pages.description: [lady climbs the glassy hill at last]

pages.caption: There she was telled of a gallant young knight that had given in some bluidy
sarks to wash, and whaever washed thae sarks was to be his wife.
The auld wife had washed till she was tired, and then she set to her
pages.scene: Old wife and daughter washing in vain

pages.caption: dochter,
pages.scene: Old wife and daughter washing in vain

pages.caption: and baith washed, and they washed, and they better washed, in hopes of getting the
pages.scene: Old wife and daughter washing in vain

pages.caption: young knight.
pages.scene: Old wife and daughter washing in vain

pages.caption: But a' they could do they couldna bring out a stain.
At length they set the stranger damosel to wark; and whenever she began the stains
came out pure and clean.
But the auld wife made the knight believe it was her dochter had washed the
pages.description: [old wife gestures to her own daughter]
pages.scene: Old wife takes credit for daughter

pages.caption: sarks.
pages.scene: Old wife takes credit for daughter

pages.caption: So the knight and the eldest dochter were to be married, and the stranger damosel
pages.scene: Knight and eldest daughter to wed

pages.caption: was distracted at the thought of it, for she was deeply in love wi' him.
pages.scene: Knight and eldest daughter to wed

pages.caption: So she bethought her of her apple, and breaking it, found it filled with gold
and precious jewelry, the richest she had ever seen.
pages.description: [gold and jewels spill from the apple]

pages.caption: "All these," she said to the eldest dochter, "I will give you, on condition that
pages.description: [lady offers jewels to the elder sister]

pages.caption: you put off your marriage for ae day, and allow me to go into his
room alone at night."
So the lady consented; but meanwhile the auld wife had prepared a sleeping-drink, and given
it to the knight, wha drank it, and never wakened till next morning.
pages.description: [knight drinks and falls into deep sleep]

pages.caption: The lee-lang night ther damosel sabbed and sang:
pages.description: [lady weeps and sings beside sleeping knight]

pages.caption: "Seven lang years I served for thee, The glassy hill I clamb for thee, The
bluidy shirt I wrang for thee; And wilt thou no wauken and turn to me?"
Next day she kentna what to do for grief.
She then brak the pear, and found it filled wi' jewelry far richer than the
pages.scene: Breaking the pear reveals richer jewels

pages.caption: contents o' the apple.
pages.scene: Breaking the pear reveals richer jewels

pages.caption: Wi' thae jewels she bargained for permission to be a second night in the young
pages.description: [lady bargains with the elder sister again]

pages.caption: knight's chamber.
But the auld wife gied him anither sleeping-drink, and he again sleepit till morning.
pages.scene: Old wife gives second sleeping potion

pages.caption: A' night she kept sighing and singing as before:
pages.scene: Second night of sighing and singing

pages.caption: But that day when he was out at the hunting, somebody asked him what noise
and moaning was yon they heard all last night in his bedchamber.
He said he heardna ony noise.
But they assured him there was sae; and he resolved to keep waking that night
to try what he could hear.
That being the third night, and the damosel being between hope and despair.
pages.description: [lady enters the chamber one last time]
pages.scene: Third night between hope and despair

pages.caption: She brak her plum, and it held far the richest jewelry of the three.
pages.scene: Breaking the plum reveals finest jewels

pages.caption: She bargained as before; and the auld wife, as before, took in the sleeping-drink to
the young knight's chamber; but he telled her he couldna drink it that night without
sweetening.
And when she gaed awa' for some honey to sweeten it wi', he poured out
pages.description: [knight pours the drink into a basin]

pages.caption: the drink,
and sae made the auld wife think he had drunk it.
pages.description: [old wife returns to find empty cup]

pages.caption: They a' went to bed again, and the damosel began, as before, singing:
"Seven lang years I served for thee, The glassy hill I clamb for thee, The
bluidy shirt I wrang for thee; And wilt thou no wauken and turn to me?"
He heard, and turned to her.
pages.scene: Knight hears and turns to her

pages.caption: And she telled him a' that had befa'en her, and he telled her a' that
pages.description: [knight and lady face each other at last]

pages.caption: had happened to him.
And he caused the auld washerwife and her dochter to be burned.
And they were married, and he and she are living happy till this day, for
pages.description: [knight and lady wed in grand ceremony]

pages.caption: aught I ken.
(1) Chambers, Popular Traditions of Scotland.
